section.title: Where Memory Ends
section.para: Everything so far scaled inside one machine: the cores of the earlier chapters share its memory, and the compiler hands them work on its own. Past the machine's edge memory is no longer shared, a message takes a fraction of a millisecond instead of a few nanoseconds, and the other side may stop answering. Scaly does not hide that edge. A for whose rounds are pure may still cross it: the runtime hands its rounds to copies of the program on other machines where that pays, as it hands them to the cores and to the graphics card. Everything else the program says itself — what goes where — and what it sends is a message.

A message is a region (): a value built on pages of its own, with everything it points to. A send ships those pages as they are, and the receiving side fixes every pointer in them to where the pages landed — with code the compiler generates for each message type. There is no serialization code to write and no schema to keep in step with the program.

section.title: A for over Machines
section.para: The program below counts the primes below three million in blocks: a plain for over the blocks, each round counting the primes of its block and putting the count in its place. Nothing in it says where its rounds run:
section.screen: $ scaly build --cluster primes.scaly -o primes $ ./primes --scaly-helper=once & $ ./primes --scaly-helper=once & $ SCALY_CLUSTER=on ./primes 216816 primes below 3000000
section.para: Built with --cluster, every for whose rounds can travel is described to the runtime — which part of the program runs a round, and what it reads and writes. Started with --scaly-helper, the same program does not run its main: it announces itself on the local network and waits for rounds. Started as it is, it is the coordinator, and where one of its loops is heavy enough it looks for helpers of its own build, hands each a stretch of rounds, runs stretches itself, and gives a helper that sends one back the next. What the rounds put comes back into the coordinator's vector; inside a stretch a helper uses its own cores, so the inner for of count_primes runs there as it would here.

Rounds travel where what they read and write can: numbers and records of numbers, vectors, slices and arrays of them read whole, and those they put into at the counter. A reduction, a value a round keeps, a string or a reference keeps the loop on this machine — nothing is said, it runs as before. The count of this program is such a reduction, and so it is added up here, after the loop that went out.

Whether a loop goes out is measured as the driver measures the cores and the card (, ): a loop that would take this machine less than 20 milliseconds is never offered; the helpers take part where, with what their stretches cost there and back, they end it a quarter sooner, and what their stretches took teaches the next offer. Here the helpers share the cores of one machine and gain nothing — the runtime would find that out and keep the loop at home —, so the transcript sends it anyway: SCALY_CLUSTER=on sends every loop that can travel, off none, and SCALY_CLUSTER_TRACE=1 shows each stretch and each decision. --scaly-helper=once ends a helper when its coordinator lets go; without it a helper serves one coordinator after the other until it is stopped.

A helper that goes — its connection closed, or silent past the heartbeat — gives its stretch back, and another runs it; with none left, the coordinator runs the rest. The rounds are pure, so the result does not depend on who ran what. Across machines the helpers hold the cluster's key and run the same build as the coordinator, as every node of this chapter does — on whatever processor, within the rule for floating point (, , ). What is not a pure loop stays explicit, and the rest of this chapter is about that.

section.title: Nodes and Channels
section.para: The same count, said explicitly, on three worker nodes. One program plays both roles: started without an argument it coordinates, with one it works. The coordinator listens on a port, hands each worker that connects a share of the range, and prints what comes back:
section.screen: $ scaly build primes.scaly -o primes $ ./primes work & $ ./primes work & $ ./primes work & $ ./primes 78498 primes from 0 to 1000000 70435 primes from 1000000 to 2000000 67883 primes from 2000000 to 3000000 216816 primes below 3000000
section.para: Here the four nodes are four processes on one machine; on four machines the workers name the coordinator's host instead of localhost, and every node is given the cluster's key (below, ). Cluster.connect keeps trying for as long as its last argument says, in milliseconds, because a worker may start before the coordinator listens; Cluster.accept waits for the next node to connect. Either answers the connection to the other node, or null.

A Remote[T] is a channel to that node for messages of one type, named by a number both sides agree on: here 1 for the shares and 2 for the counts. send hands a message over and returns at once; receive waits for the next one and answers it, or null when the other node has said goodbye or is gone. Cluster.disconnect says goodbye. The coordinator first sends every share and only then collects, so the three workers count at the same time — and each of them counts its share with the plain for of , on all the cores of its machine.

section.title: A Message Is a Region
section.para: counts.send(Count(n, "…")) builds the Count — the record and the string in it — on a page of its own, and the send ships that page and releases it. What is sent is gone from the sender; nothing on the other side can point back into it. The receiving node's pages hold the same bytes at other addresses, the generated code fixes the pointers, and receive hands the message to the routine that asked: it belongs to that routine's region from then on and goes when that region goes, like any value the routine built itself.

Because the send builds the message, its argument is the construction, or a call that makes the message. A value built before would have its string on another page, which the send would not ship, so a name is refused:
section.programlisting: let c Count(n, "`share.from` to `share.to`") counts.send(c) ; error: send builds the message on a page of its own
section.para: A message may hold records, unions, strings and the containers of the standard library — Vector, Array, List, HashMap — nested as deep as the program likes. What only makes sense in one process cannot be sent, and the compiler says so: a delegate, an open file, a fixed-size array.

section.title: One Program, One Build
section.para: Pages shipped as they are only make sense to a program that lays out its records the same way. So the nodes of a cluster run one build of one program — which is why the transcript builds once and starts the result four times. Two nodes check it before anything else: each sends a stamp of its build when it connects, and a node whose stamp differs is refused, with both stamps in the error. A new version of the program is a new cluster.

The stamp is taken from the program as the compiler emits it, before it becomes one processor's instructions, so it does not name the processor or the system. The same source built with the same compiler for an arm64 Mac, an x86_64 Linux server or an arm64 Linux board has one stamp, and their nodes form one cluster: on all of them a record is laid out alike — 64-bit pointers, little-endian —, and the nodes tell each other so when they connect. A Windows PC joins them too: what its linker needs on top is left out of the stamp. A build for WebAssembly, with pointers of four bytes, joins only its own kind.

section.title: The Same Bits on Every Processor
section.para: A round must compute the same on a helper as at home, or the result would depend on who ran what. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and the square root are rounded exactly as IEEE 754 says on every processor, and the compiler never fuses a multiplication with an addition on its own. The C library's exp, sin or log are another matter: each system approximates them its own way, and the last bit differs between them. So the standard library brings its own, written in Scaly from those exact operations: exp, exp2, expm1, log, log2, log10, log1p, sin, cos, tan, atan, atan2, asin, acos, pow, hypot, cbrt, sinh, cosh and tanh, for f64 and f32. Their result is the double nearest to the exact value for nearly every argument, and never more than about 0.52 units in the last place from it. They are generic, so each is made in the program that calls it: put in line, and a loop over it can use the processor's vector lanes.
section.programlisting: let x 0.5 print "`exp(x)` `log(x)` `sin(x)` `cos(x)`" print "`pow(2.0, x)` `atan2(1.0, 1.0) * 4.0`" let bits sin(x).to_bits() print "`bits`"
section.para: The last line is what every processor of one class prints. The classes are two, and one operation tells them apart: x.mul_add(y, z), x * y + z with one rounding where the processor has a fused multiply-add — an arm64 processor always, an x86_64 one from Haswell on, in a build for -mcpu=x86-64-v3 or -mcpu=native on such a machine — and with two where it has not: a build for the generic x86_64, and WebAssembly. The functions above use it, so they come in two flavours from one source. With the fused operation they compute the same bits everywhere; without it they are relaxed, as fast and within one unit in the last place (two for tan, atan2 and hypot), but not the same bits. x.mul_error(y), the rounding error of a product, is exact in both: where a result would suffer — pow — the library uses it.

Each node announces its class when it is found and when it connects. A loop whose rounds call mul_add — themselves or through exp, sin and the rest — goes only to helpers of the coordinator's class; every other loop goes to every helper, other loops of the same program too. Written relaxed (), such a loop may go to the other class as well, and its results may then differ in the last bits, as on a card under WebGPU:
section.programlisting: for i in n out.put(i, exp(xs[i])) ; to helpers of this machine's class relaxed for i in n out.put(i, exp(xs[i])) ; to every helper
section.para: The tests of the cluster runtime run an arm64 Mac as the coordinator with x86_64 helpers under Rosetta 2. A helper built for Haswell takes every loop, and the results are the same to the last bit as on the Mac alone; one built for the generic x86_64 takes the loops without mul_add and the relaxed one, and leaves the strict loop with exp to the Mac.

section.title: When a Node Fails
section.para: A node that crashes, loses its network or stops answering looks the same from the other side as one that said goodbye: its channels close, and a receive waiting on one of them answers null. That is why the coordinator asks if c <> null: with a worker killed in the middle of its share it prints the counts of the others and finishes. A silent node is noticed by its silence — the nodes exchange a heartbeat every half second when nothing else flows, and one silent for two and a half seconds is taken for gone. That is a suspicion, not a proof; a node that was only slow finds its connection closed.

A send never waits for an answer and is never retried: a message arrives at most once, the messages of one channel in the order they were sent, and a message sent to a node that is gone is dropped. Whether a lost share is sent to another worker is the program's decision, not the runtime's. The tests of the cluster runtime include such a program: a small transformer trained on several nodes, each computing the gradients of its part of a batch, one node summing them in a fixed order and sending the sum back. Its loss is the same to the last bit as on one node, and with one worker killed mid-run the others finish the training.

Who may join is decided before the first message. A cluster without a key stays on one machine: a node listens on the loopback only and refuses a peer from anywhere else. Across machines every node holds the same key — in the environment as SCALY_CLUSTER_KEY, or in the file ~/.scaly/cluster.key — and proves it when it connects, by an HMAC over a challenge of the other side; a node with another key, or none, is refused. One limit is named: the key keeps strangers out, it does not hide what the nodes say to each other. The messages are not encrypted, and a node checks the framing of what it receives, not the meaning — run a cluster across machines only inside a network you trust.
